instruction.text: First read this journal article on the Giant’s Causeway. Then answer the questions.

atoms.text: Northern Ireland’s coastline is defined by its many fascinating stone formations, but none is more famous than the Giant’s Causeway. It is a 4-mile-long, unique rock formation consisting of more than 40,000 hexagonal-shaped columns of rock. Over the centuries, many legends and myths evolved to explain its existence, but the causeway wasn’t really created by giants — there’s a perfectly good scientific explanation.
atoms.sound: Northern Ireland’s coastline is defined by its many fascinating stone formations, but none is more famous than the Giant’s Causeway. It is a 4-mile-long, unique rock formation consisting of more than 40,000 hexagonal-shaped columns of rock. Over the centuries, many legends and myths evolved to explain its existence, but the causeway wasn’t really created by giants — there’s a perfectly good scientific explanation.

atoms.text: About 60 million years ago, the area that is now the Giant’s Causeway experienced intense volcanic activity. Geologists believe that a volcanic eruption produced large amounts of lava that spread out over a wide area and cooled, forming a lava plateau.
atoms.sound: About 60 million years ago, the area that is now the Giant’s Causeway experienced intense volcanic activity. Geologists believe that a volcanic eruption produced large amounts of lava that spread out over a wide area and cooled, forming a lava plateau.

atoms.text: As the molten rock hit the surface of the sea, it began cooling very quickly. This drastic change in temperature produced a unique effect — the lava contracted and condensed until thousands of vertical cracks emerged and 40,000 other similarly shaped stone columns were created. Talk about a force of nature!

atoms.text: On the Scottish side of the Giant’s Causeway sits the Isle of Staffa, an island formed from the same hexagonal rock columns as found on the Northern Irish coastline. The distance between these two locations shows just how powerful the eruption must have been. Today, all the volcanoes in the area are extinct and both ends of the Giant’s Causeway are popular tourist attractions.

instruction.text: What is the scientific explanation for the Giant’s Causeway? Bring the events into the correct order by matching the photo with the corresponding text.

atoms.b: First, there was a lot of volcanic activity around the area that would become the Giant’s Causeway.
The volcanic eruption produced large amounts of lava.
The lava spread out over a huge area, building a lava plateau.
The temperature of the lava changed very quickly.
The cooling lava condensed and formed thousands of hexagonal-shaped columns of rock.
